stories.title: Malaysia to start electricity market for data centre operators
stories.summary: Malaysia plans to create a dedicated wholesale electricity market specifically designed for large power consumers such as data center operators, allowing them to negotiate directly with generators rather than purchasing through the national utility Tenaga Nasional Berhad. The New Straits Times reported that this reform aims to improve price transparency and supply reliability for energy-intensive digital infrastructure investments.
stories.why_it_matters: A separate wholesale market would decouple data center power economics from residential and industrial tariff structures, potentially delivering 15-25% cost reductions for hyperscale operators. This fundamentally alters Malaysia's competitive position against Singapore, where power costs remain regulated and high. However, implementation complexity is substantial—grid balancing, renewable energy certificate tracking, and contract enforcement mechanisms must be established. If successful, Johor and Sarawak could see accelerated land acquisition for campus-style developments; if delayed, investors may revert to on-site gas generation, undermining national emissions targets.

stories.content:
(Nov 11): Malaysia intends to launch a separate wholesale electricity market for large power consumers, including data centres, the *New Straits Times* reported.

The existing single-buyer market serving households, factories and commercial premises will stay the same, the newspaper said, citing Rumaizi Abdul Halim, director of market regulation and planning at Malaysia’s Energy Commission. The two markets will run under a single operator but details on how they would interact will be discussed later, he said on Tuesday.

The move underscores Malaysia’s efforts to deal with the potential fallout from its ambitious push to become a regional hub for data centres. The Southeast Asian country has attracted artificial intelligence investment from technology heavyweights, including Oracle Corp and Amazon.com Inc, while Alphabet Inc’s Google said last week that it plans to spend US$15 billion (RM61.12 billion) to expand data centre and cloud operations in Malaysia.

stories.title: Global policies target data-centre grid delays, lower emissions
stories.summary: Governments worldwide are implementing policies to accelerate grid connections for data centers and reduce their growing reliance on on-site natural gas generation, which threatens to increase carbon emissions from AI-driven infrastructure growth, according to BloombergNEF research. These measures include streamlined permitting for transmission upgrades, direct utility partnerships, and carbon intensity requirements for new facilities.
stories.why_it_matters: For APAC markets where data center demand is surging fastest—Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and parts of Australia—grid connection timelines often exceed 24-36 months, driving operators toward gas peaking plants as interim solutions. The global policy momentum documented by BNEF creates leverage for national regulators to mandate cleaner alternatives, but only if accompanied by actual transmission investment. Operators face a strategic bifurcation: those securing renewable power purchase agreements and grid priority access will command premium pricing from carbon-conscious multinational tenants; those defaulting to gas may face stranded asset risk as emissions disclosure requirements tighten across supply chains.

stories.title_zh: Global policies target data-centre grid delays, lower emissions
stories.summary_zh: 据BloombergNEF研究，全球各国政府正在实施政策以加速数据中心的电网连接，并减少其对现场天然气发电的日益依赖，这种依赖威胁到增加AI驱动基础设施增长带来的碳排放。这些措施包括输电升级的简化许可、直接公用事业合作伙伴关系以及对新设施的碳强度要求。
stories.why_zh: 对于数据中心需求增长最快的亚太市场——马来西亚、印度尼西亚、泰国和澳大利亚部分地区——电网连接时间通常超过24-36个月，推动运营商选择天然气调峰电厂作为临时解决方案。BNEF记录的全球政策势头为国家监管机构强制要求更清洁的替代方案创造了杠杆，但前提是有实际的输电投资伴随。运营商面临战略分化：那些获得可再生能源购电协议和电网优先接入权的运营商将从具有碳意识的跨国租户那里获得溢价定价；那些默认使用天然气的运营商可能面临随着供应链排放披露要求收紧而产生的搁浅资产风险。
stories.content:
Data-centre developers are increasingly turning to so-called behind-the-meter power generation to bypass years-long waits for grid connections and get their facilities running sooner. Those systems typically rely on natural gas, potentially reversing years of progress in cutting emissions from electricity generation.

A report published Wednesday by BNEF examines proposed policy efforts in the US, Europe and Asia to accelerate grid connections and limit the environmental impact of data-centre growth.

“Powering data centers via the grid today would result in lower CO2 emissions than using on-site gas in the US and Europe,” the report’s authors wrote. “Keeping data centres connected to the grid in developed markets is therefore a core pillar of keeping them green.”

BNEF’s report comes as the annual UN Climate Change Conference, COP31, gets underway in Antalya, Türkiye. The environmental footprint of data-centre expansion is expected to feature in discussions among world leaders, government officials and financial industry executives seeking ways to accelerate the transition to cleaner energy.

Bankers have already said AI will be part of “every conversation” at the summit. Even so, the scale of AI’s climate impact remains difficult to quantify. Data-centre electricity demand is likely to quadruple by 2035, reaching about 7% of global power consumption, according to BNEF estimates.

The BNEF report, commissioned by Bloomberg Philanthropies, assessed seven different policy types aimed at speeding up data centres’ grid connections. Four showed strong evidence of accelerating those connections, while only two were found to have a direct impact on increasing the supply of clean energy for data centres.

“The bottom line here is it depends on what each power market needs,” said Musfika Mishi, a BNEF analyst and co-author of the report.

For example, at PJM Interconnection, the largest US grid operator, there is a huge deficit in supply, so the company is “prioritising policies that get data centres connected to the grid faster, but also bring supply to the grid,” she said.

Not every policy analysed in the report is explicitly designed to make data-centre power supplies cleaner, Mishi said. But in developed markets, connecting to the grid is generally better for the climate than relying on on-site generation, she said.

The report also acknowledges that most policies to speed up grid connections are too new to assess how much they actually shorten wait times or reduce emissions. Still, the policies proposed represent an important step towards addressing the challenge of expanding data-centre capacity without driving up greenhouse gas emissions.

“You’ve got a balance between affordability, reliability and sustainability, that classic trilemma. And I think in recent years there’s been a bit more focus on affordability and reliability rather than sustainability,” said Derrick Flakoll, a BNEF analyst and co-author of the report. “I would say that in certain places like the US, where you’ve had different election results, those are going to continue to be big themes.”

BNEF also examined data-centre growth in developing markets, where the challenge is often shifting power systems towards cleaner energy while expanding the infrastructure needed to serve new demand.

In India, for example, that means adding local transmission and substation capacity fast enough to keep pace with data-centre development. In Malaysia, data-centre growth is expected to increase reliance on existing coal and gas plants in the near term.

stories.title: Cohere in a 'fight' to secure AI computing power
stories.summary: (Nov 11): Cohere Inc chief executive officer Aidan Gomez pushed back on concerns about overbuilding AI computing capacity, saying his startup faces a daily struggle to procure the power it needs to run its operations.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Cohere "奋力" securing AI computing power
stories.content:
The Canadian startup, an Nvidia Corp.-backed developer of artificial intelligence models for businesses, is confronting shortages of what the industry calls compute, the sheer computational power needed to churn through the training and operation of models. Without its own data centers, Cohere depends on cloud providers like the big names like Microsoft Corp’s Azure or the so-called neocloud providers like CoreWeave Inc.

“We really have to fight to get access to compute,” Gomez said in an interview with *Bloomberg* in Tokyo on Wednesday. “There is a dearth of supply. We need much more compute. We need the energy, the facilities, the chips to support that.”

Gomez is visiting Japan this week to help expand Cohere’s business with Japanese enterprise customers and government agencies. His comments underscore demand for AI chips and processing, which was also highlighted by CoreWeave’s robust earnings overnight. CoreWeave reported better-than-expected sales of US$3.66 billion for the September quarter, helped by growing relationships with clients including Cohere.

“We might be over-indexing to fear in this present moment, but hopefully the build-out continues, and those supply pressures do alleviate,” Gomez said.

He’s added his voice to a global debate about the intensity of spending on building out AI data centres, which are coming in for greater skepticism as costs rise, projects run into unforeseen challenges and communities increasingly protest the setup of such facilities in their locales. SoftBank Group Corp on Tuesday announced it was writing down US$3.7 billion in costs associated with its US data centre projects, as the company best known for its investments transitions into a hardware and infrastructure developer.

Toronto-based Cohere, which seeks to sell its services in support of countries pursuing sovereign AI, last month raised as much as US$5 billion in a funding round valuing it at more than US$20 billion.

Cohere and Nvidia are working together to develop custom AI models optimised for the US chipmaker’s platforms. Gomez described the recent revelations about Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s infidelity as “a really unfortunate episode” — one that would deal a great blow if he’s forced to step down from his post. Huang’s extramarital affair is being probed by the FBI and Nvidia-appointed independent investigators over allegations it may have been with a Chinese spy.

“Any change of leadership, especially with someone as effective, and with such a strong vision as Jensen would be quite disruptive,” he said. “Jensen has been leading the company for 30 years, it’s his vision that really carried it to the place that it is today.”

stories.summary: The recent sell-off in YTL Power International Bhd (KL:YTLPOWR) appears excessive as its colocation data centre business continues to support the group's valuation, said CGS International.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: CGS International称YTL Power抛售过度，对data centre前景保持乐观
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 11): The recent sell-off in YTL Power International Bhd (KL:YTLPOWR) appears excessive as its colocation data centre business continues to support the group's valuation, said CGS International.

CGS kept its ‘add’ rating and RM6.50 target price on YTL Power, staying bullish despite pressure from Nvidia-related concerns and tighter scrutiny of artificial intelligence (AI) chip supply chains.

The research house cited improving near-term earnings and longer-term growth prospects that it believes are not fully reflected in the share price.

“We believe it is important to distinguish YTL Power’s contracted colocation business from its broader AI data centre ambitions.

“Our RM6.50 target price does not attribute any material value to a successful ramp-up of the AI data centre business, with our data centre valuation primarily based on 850MW of assumed colocation capacity.

“As such, any hiccups in scaling up the AI data centre business would have limited direct impact on our current earnings forecasts and valuation,” it said in a note on Wednesday.

YTL Power shares fell 6.4% to close at RM4.69 on Tuesday amid renewed scrutiny of its data centre partner Nvidia over espionage allegations.

The counter has declined 21% since end-September, weighed down by broader global data centre concerns, heightened US regulatory uncertainty following the midterm elections and Indonesian gas curtailments affecting its Singapore-based power generation unit, PowerSeraya.

At the time of writing on Wednesday, the counter had gained six sen or 1.28% to RM4.75, with 1.92 million shares traded, giving the group a market capitalisation of RM41.74 billion.

CGS said the recent decline in data centre valuations has mainly affected neocloud and hybrid operators, whose enterprise value to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization multiples have fallen by about 37% since end-September 2026.

In comparison, listed colocation data centre operators have been more resilient, with the broader peer group declining by only 5%, while those outside Hong Kong and China have remained broadly unchanged.

This is relevant to YTL Power, as its data centre valuation is primarily supported by its colocation business, which has 298MW of existing contracted capacity, rather than the more volatile AI and neocloud segments, it said.

Meanwhile, CGS expects stronger Singapore spark spreads to contribute about RM35 million to YTL Power's quarterly earnings, largely offsetting the estimated RM38 million impact of Indonesian gas curtailments on PowerSeraya in the second quarter of the financial year ending June 30, 2027 (2QFY2027).

“We have updated our earnings model to reflect YTL Power’s recently released FY2026 annual report and other developments, as well as the recent improvement in Singapore spark spreads and higher PowerSeraya volume assumptions following the completion of maintenance shutdowns in 1H2026. This results in a 6.5% increase in our net profit forecast for FY2027F,” it said.

Beyond the near-term earnings recovery, CGS sees further growth potential from the progressive commissioning of secured data centre capacity, additional capacity wins and the deployment of YTL Power's reserved gas turbines to meet rising electricity demand in Malaysia and the wider region.

The research house also said tighter US regulatory scrutiny and power constraints could encourage some data centre workloads to shift to other markets.

"As highlighted in a report last week by our partner Raymond James, the evolving US policy environment is likely to place greater emphasis on power availability, project approvals and infrastructure readiness, rather than necessarily curtailing AI capex outright.

"This could support spillover demand for non-latency-sensitive workloads towards locations with ready land, infra and faster time-to-market — these dynamics play into YTL Power's strengths, in our view,” it added.

stories.title_zh: SoftBank股价在减记70亿美元亏损后波动
stories.content:
(Nov 11): SoftBank Group Corp shares fluctuated as investors assessed its quarterly net loss and a US$3.7 billion (RM15.1 billion) writedown over its US data centres, against newfound optimism around artificial intelligence (AI).

The stock fell as much as 11% in early trading in Tokyo. The Japanese tech investor said Tuesday it swung to a ¥1.12 trillion (US$7.1 billion or RM29 billion) loss in its fiscal second quarter after writing down non-refundable advance payments it made to secure power-generation equipment for its US data centres.

The stock rose as much as 0.8% in the afternoon as the sentiment for the sector got a boost from better-than-expected earnings from AI computing provider CoreWeave Inc and a report that Anthropic PBC’s bankers are weighing plans to increase the company’s valuation in its initial public offering.

“What investors worried about most this past week was whether data centre investment would slow,” said Toshiro Sato, a chief executive officer at Kyokuto Securities Research Institute. “SoftBank’s results came as everyone was anxious about that business. After the selling ran its course, the reassessment came through and the stock is coming back.”

SoftBank had previously hurried to secure the equipment it needed for AI data centres, sometimes even before long-term plans were finalised, chief financial officer Yoshimitsu Goto said during an earnings conference.

Total payments for power-generation equipment hit US$9.5 billion by September, he said. The company said in its earnings statement that it can receive rebates of up to US$2.1 billion over the next 10 years on future equipment purchases. SoftBank is conducting “a thorough reassessment” including a review of its procurement strategy, Goto said, without going into specifics.

While part of the loss is due to accounting, “the real issues are a ¥597 billion power-equipment write-off that raised more questions” than what the management could explain, and the financing costs that grew 2.6 times year-on-year, Jefferies analyst Atul Goyal wrote in a note. “Management is playing defence.”

SoftBank shares have plunged more than 50% from their record high in June, among the worst performers on the Nikkei 225 Stock Average for the period. Volatility, meanwhile, has risen as investors sought to gauge the risks and opportunities around its AI investments.

stories.title: DeepSeek, other China AI firms have just 10% the revenue of OpenAI, Anthropic
stories.summary: Chinese AI companies including DeepSeek collectively generate approximately 10% of the revenue achieved by leading American firms OpenAI and Anthropic, despite comparable technical capabilities in certain model benchmarks. The revenue gap reflects structural challenges including limited international market access, domestic price competition, and US chip export controls that constrain training scale and commercial deployment.
stories.why_it_matters: The revenue disparity exposes the commercial limitations of China's AI sector even as its technical output advances, with implications for APAC data center demand patterns. Chinese AI firms' constrained scaling means less incremental demand for overseas GPU clusters and international colocation capacity, redirecting infrastructure investment toward domestic facilities. For Southeast Asian markets positioning as neutral AI hubs, the gap represents opportunity—enterprises seeking alternatives to both US and Chinese models may drive demand for sovereign inference infrastructure, particularly in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Vietnam where data localization requirements are strengthening.

stories.title: SPECIAL FEATURE: Aye robots: The exciting new world of physical AI
stories.summary: Modern data centers are power intensive, and the growing demand for AI computing creates a challenge for operators to maintain physical infrastructure, manage dense GPU deployments, optimize cooling systems and ensure uninterrupted operations. Robotics and physical AI offers a potential solution by automating repetitive physical tasks, improving operational efficiency, increasing safety and enabling effective facility […]
stories.title_zh: 特别报道 | Aye robots：physical AI的激动人心的新世界
stories.content:
Modern data centers are power intensive, and the growing demand for AI computing creates a challenge for operators to maintain physical infrastructure, manage dense GPU deployments, optimize cooling systems and ensure uninterrupted operations. Robotics and physical AI offers a potential solution by automating repetitive physical tasks, improving operational efficiency, increasing safety and enabling effective facility management. This deployment of automatic management could change data center operations from labour intensive maintenance towards predictive and autonomous operations.

In this special feature, we explore how robotic automation in data centers can perform a variety of tasks to increase efficiency and optimize operations. These include conducting infrastructure inspections, transporting heavy server equipment, monitoring cooling systems, identifying potential equipment failures and operating in hazardous environments. Equipped with technologies such as computer vision, thermal imaging, LiDAR and artificial intelligence which collects operational data, detects anomalies and prevents infrastructure failures.

#### **What makes physical AI exciting?**

Physical AI represents a new stage of intelligent data center infrastructure that extends artificial intelligence beyond data processing into the physical machines. By combining AI with robotics, computer vision, sensors, digital twins, and autonomous control systems, machines can perceive and perform physical tasks. This convergence has the potential to transform data center operations, maintenance, security, and energy efficiency while reducing reliance on human intervention.

Key applications include autonomous robots for equipment inspection, fault detection, and hardware maintenance, as well as AI driven cooling systems that optimize airflow and liquid cooling based on real time conditions. Digital twins enable predictive maintenance and infrastructure optimization, while autonomous security systems enhance surveillance, intrusion detection, and personnel safety.

“GenAI amplifies how enterprises think; physical AI transforms how they operate,” Parm Sandhu (Group Vice President: Enterprise 5G Products and Services, NTT DATA), told w.media in a recent exclusive interview. “It moves intelligence off the screen and into machines and operations where the largest enterprise value pools sit: manufacturing, logistics, energy, mining. This is not a hypothetical shift.”

The physical AI sector is attracting significant investment, with major deals and funding rounds indicating a growing demand for computing infrastructure and AI-powered robotics. According to report by Fortune Business Insight, the global physical AI market was valued at US$ 33.42 billion in 2025, and is projected to grow from US$ 42.06 billion in 2026, to US$ 294.07 billion by 2034, registering a CAGR of 27.5 percent during the forecast period.

North America dominated the market in 2025, accounting for a 35.06 percent share. By integrating AI models with sensors, physics-aware reasoning, simulation technologies, and actuators, it enables applications such as robotics, autonomous vehicles, drones, and intelligent machinery to make autonomous decisions, perform physical tasks, and adapt to changing real-world conditions while accounting for physical constraints, time, safety, and uncertainty.

Among recent developments, Nscale and Figure have signed a multi-year partnership with humanoid robotics, committing an initial US$ 3.5 billion in AI computing capacity, with plans to expand the deal to more than US$ 6 billion. The agreement could involve deploying up to 100,000 NVIDIA GPUs to support the development and scaling of Figure’s AI models and humanoid robots, with the initial deployment expected in the second half of 2027.

“Humanoid robots extend physical AI into the world designed for people—opening a major new industry,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO, NVIDIA. “Nscale and Figure have activated the robotics flywheel: training Figure’s models on NVIDIA Vera Rubin through Nscale’s AI cloud, validating them in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, and deploying them on NVIDIA GPUs in Figure’s robots. This is the physical AI flywheel that will accelerate the path from models to robots in the world.”

In a separate development, LG Electronics and NVIDIA are planning to establish an AI factory in Seoul to support robotics and industrial AI development. While financial details of the LG-NVIDIA initiative have not been disclosed, the facility will provide infrastructure for AI training, simulation, validation and deployment. The facility will have four floors covering 10,000 square meters to house several hundred robots.

The evolution toward autonomous data centers will progress through five stages: instrumented infrastructure, AI-assisted operations, autonomous physical inspection, AI-driven physical intervention, and ultimately self-optimizing facilities. At this final stage, integrated AI agents, robotics, digital twins, and autonomous controls will coordinate operations, anticipate failures, and continuously optimize performance within defined safety boundaries. Physical AI will be a key enabler of more resilient, efficient, and intelligent data centers.

#### **Cloud providers embrace robotics**

Cloud providers are increasingly exploring robotics to automate data center operations as infrastructure grows in scale and complexity. The focus is shifting beyond equipment transportation and inspection towards hardware maintenance, component replacement and lifecycle management. Meta and Microsoft are among the companies developing and testing robotic systems for these applications.

Meta has deployed autonomous robots for server rack transportation, inventory management and equipment inspections, while testing robotic arms for cabling, server power cycling and hardware handling.

Microsoft, through its Creative Robotics and Future Technologies (CRAFT) research programme, is developing robots capable of identifying and replacing optical transceivers, as well as performing optical-fibre cleaning and installation. Its longer term objective is to automate the hardware lifecycle, from rack assembly and deployment to maintenance, repair and decommissioning.

The development of data center robotics is also supported by wider advances in AI and industrial automation. Agile Robots SE and Google DeepMind have partnered to combine Gemini Robotics foundation models with industrial robotics hardware, targeting more adaptable robots capable of performing complex tasks.

NVIDIA and LG Group are similarly developing an AI factory to support the development, simulation and deployment of physical AI systems across robotics, autonomous driving and data centers. ABB Robotics and US start-up Molg are developing robotic microfactories to automate the disassembly and recycling of data center equipment, supporting component recovery and reducing electronic waste.

The data centers of the future will evolve into a highly coordinated physical AI ecosystem in which intelligent machines, autonomous robots, AI agents, and human engineers work together. Autonomous robots will increasingly support equipment inspection, security patrols, hardware logistics, and selected maintenance activities, while intelligent control systems optimize cooling, power distribution, and infrastructure performance.

More advanced applications may eventually include robotic server replacement, automated fiber-optic cable management, and humanoid robots performing selected maintenance tasks, although these capabilities are still emerging. The real opportunity is not simply replacing people with robots, but creating an intelligent, self-monitoring, self-optimizing, and increasingly self-maintaining data center.

stories.content:
Virtual power plants (VPPs) are becoming a core grid resource, moving into mainstream grid planning during 2025 and 2026. This shift means VPPs are now a genuine flexibility resource for utilities and grid operators managing rising demand and a decentralising generation mix.The aggregated resources for VPPs have broadened beyond rooftop solar and home resources. Managed electric vehicle (EV) charging providers are partnering with solar aggregators and smart energy ecosystem providers. This brings charging infrastructure and vehicles into the resource mix alongside photovoltaics.Battery energy storage systems (BESS), a fast-growing distributed energy resource (DER) category, are also feeding directly into VPP portfolios. Sunrun, Tesla Energy, and Renew Home partnered to aggregate over 16 GW of residential batteries and smart thermostats. This project uses OpenADR 2.0b to communicate demand response signals and will sell capacity directly to hyperscale data center operators.Commercial building management is following a similar trend. Modern VPP implementations involve an edge gateway in a building’s server room, connected to operational technology (OT) protocols like BACnet and Modbus. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted classification then builds a data model with granularity down to one- to 15-minute intervals.The software layer distinguishes this new generation of VPPs from earlier deployments. Advanced cloud-based platforms, combined with AI-driven forecasting and load balancing, monitor and optimise diverse resources. This enables a portfolio spanning solar, storage, EV charging, heat pumps, and commercial building loads to function as a single coordinated resource. Bi-directional communication among components tightens systems for grid operators.Open, interoperable standards are essential for VPPs to communicate reliably with dispatching systems. This ensures a signal from a utility or independent system operator (ISO) is understood uniformly across different vendors’ equipment. This interoperability is crucial for scaling VPPs at a reasonable price.Regulatory requirements are also reinforcing market growth. California’s 2023 compensation rule changes for Community Choice Aggregators (CCAs) prompted CCAs to explore VPPs. These VPPs can create new value for buildings and support grid reliability. VPPs require the same planning discipline as any other flexible capacity resource, including clear visibility and confidence in communication standards.

stories.title_zh: 工业AI推动small modular reactors走向商业化现实
stories.content:
Small modular reactors (SMRs) are becoming a critical component of the future power mix, fueled by increasing electricity demand and the grid’s struggle to expand sufficiently. These advanced nuclear fission plants are significantly smaller than traditional reactors, requiring less capital and offering faster deployment times.SMRs provide low-carbon power that does not depend on weather conditions for reliable generation. They can be constructed underground, enhancing resilience against extreme weather events like earthquakes, and can start up without external grid energy. This makes them suitable for remote regions with less developed infrastructure and attractive to energy-intensive industries and large commercial users.
### Deployment and Challenges

Multiple smaller SMR units can be deployed together to meet the power demands of large industrial facilities or data centers. This modular design allows for flexible expansion of generation capacity over time. However, challenges remain, including the existence of over 80 global SMR designs and concepts, which complicates standardization and cross-border scaling.Regulatory requirements also vary by country or region, adding complexity to deployment. Despite these hurdles, global government support from nations such as the UK, US, and the European Commission is shifting SMRs from concept to commercial reality. Companies like Rolls-Royce are also developing their own commercial SMR designs.
### AI in Lifecycle Management

Industrial AI and software are essential for managing the full lifecycle of SMRs. This includes planning investments, determining optimal locations and capacities, and building return on investment cases. During construction, AI assists with procurement, supply chain coordination, and workforce management.Once operational, AI-driven monitoring ensures efficiency and public safety compliance, meeting regulatory and community demands. At the end of an SMR's life, the same lifecycle approach, supported by AI, extends to decommissioning and recycling processes. These AI advancements are critical as organisations balance decarbonisation goals with the immediate need for reliable and affordable energy.

stories.content:
Wed, 11th Nov 2026 (Today)
AMD has launched its 6th Gen EPYC server processors and the new EPYC Embedded 9006 Series. The server chips are now shipping in systems from major hardware vendors.

The new server range is based on AMD's Zen 6 architecture and targets data centre workloads across enterprise applications, cloud computing, high-performance computing and AI.

AMD said the 6th Gen EPYC portfolio is designed for different CPU roles in AI infrastructure, including general-purpose services, GPU host nodes and agent sandbox environments. Cloud deployments are planned across major providers, including Microsoft Azure and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

In benchmarks cited by AMD, the top-end EPYC 9996 chip delivered up to 2.2 times the performance of Intel's Xeon 6980P and up to 3.7 times the performance of Nvidia's Vera CPU. AMD also said the line offers up to about 3.3 times the agents-per-watt of Nvidia Vera for agentic AI workloads.

Those claims come as chipmakers try to define the CPU's role in AI systems that also rely heavily on accelerators. AMD's position is that processors remain central to orchestration, data access, enterprise applications and host functions around AI models.

"AI is significantly expanding the role of the CPU across every layer of the data center," said Dan McNamara, Senior Vice President and General Manager, Compute and Enterprise AI, AMD. "With 6th Gen AMD EPYC, customers can standardize on the proven x86 foundation while choosing a workload-optimized solution to run more agents, keep accelerated infrastructure fed and power the business-critical applications they depend on."

### Cloud rollout

Server systems using the processors are shipping from leading original equipment manufacturers and original design manufacturers, according to AMD. Meta is working with AMD as a lead customer and has been validating platforms based on the new chips ahead of wider deployment.

Microsoft Azure is preparing several services tied to the new processors, including Azure HDv2 for AI data processing, agentic AI and high-performance computing, and Azure HXv2 for electronic design automation and technical computing. Azure ND MI455X v7, based on AMD Helios, is also cited for production-scale AI inference.

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is also set to use the processors in OCI Compute E7 instances for enterprise applications and CPU tasks surrounding AI models. AMD presented the breadth of support as evidence that the product line is aimed at both conventional enterprise computing and newer AI-linked infrastructure.

### Embedded push

Alongside the server announcement, AMD introduced the EPYC Embedded 9006 Series for applications such as semiconductor test equipment, network security and enterprise storage. The chips offer up to 256 cores, next-generation connectivity and seven-year product longevity, according to AMD.

The embedded release broadens the reach of the EPYC brand beyond mainstream server deployments at a time when processor vendors are trying to capture demand across a wider range of infrastructure categories. Buyers in embedded markets often prioritise long support cycles and stable supply as much as raw compute performance.

### Rack strategy

AMD also outlined its Helion rack approach for AI deployments, with liquid-cooled and air-cooled designs as well as a configuration that combines CPU execution with local GPU inference in one rack. Some configurations can reach up to 73,728 threads in a single rack, according to AMD.

The pitch reflects growing interest in rack-level design rather than standalone server performance as operators seek to balance compute density, energy use, cooling and networking. Across the market, suppliers are increasingly packaging CPUs, GPUs and interconnects as integrated infrastructure rather than separate components.

AMD's latest launch extends a product line that has steadily gained share in the server market over several generations. The company said its 5th Gen EPYC family was the fastest-ramping and highest-volume EPYC generation in its history, setting the backdrop for this release.

For customers assessing server platforms, the key questions will centre on performance under real workloads, energy use, system availability and software support across existing estates. Systems powered by 6th Gen EPYC server processors are shipping from leading server vendors, AMD said.

stories.title: Thailand approves new data center rules on noise, heat, zoning, and cooling
stories.summary: Thailand's Cabinet has approved comprehensive new regulations governing data center operations, establishing strict limits on noise emissions to 70 dBA at facility boundaries and restricting temperature increases in surrounding areas to 1-2 degrees Celsius. The rules also mandate cooling water recirculation and pre-discharge testing, while introducing zoning requirements that will restrict where large power-consuming facilities can be located.
stories.why_it_matters: Thailand's regulatory codification provides investment certainty that has been absent as speculative projects multiplied without clear permitting standards, but the noise and thermal restrictions may effectively exclude dense urban locations like central Bangkok. This pushes development toward industrial zones in Eastern Economic Corridor provinces, where land is available but fiber latency to major business districts increases. For international operators, the rules create compliance benchmarks comparable to Singapore's, potentially elevating Thailand's attractiveness for risk-averse institutional investors who previously favored more mature markets.

stories.summary_zh: 泰国内阁已批准全面规范数据中心运营的新法规，将设施边界的噪音排放限制在70 dBA，并将周边地区的温度升高限制在1-2摄氏度。这些规则还强制要求冷却水循环和排放前测试，同时引入分区要求，限制高耗电设施的位置。

stories.content:
Thailand’s Cabinet has yesterday approved new rules to limit noise at data center boundaries to 70 A-weighted decibels (dBA), and capping nearby temperature increases to 1 – 2 degrees Celsius, according to a government data center board. It also proposed that cooling water must be recirculated and tested before discharge.

In addition, data centers consuming more than 20MW of energy must be located in industrial zones with more stringent oversight under new zoning rules, Danucha Pichayanan, secretary-general of Thailand’s economic planning agency reportedly said after the Cabinet’s approval.

The new rules came about after Thailand paused the construction of 49 data centers due to complaints over environmental and community safety.

According to a Yale University chart comparison, the 70dBA is “slightly quieter than a vacuum cleaner.”

Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas had reportedly said projects that fail to meet security and environmental requirements “will not be allowed to proceed”.

Thailand’s Board of Investment meanwhile said it has approved 57 data center projects nationwide. Out of that, 17 are operating, 20 have received construction permits and 20 are preparing to invest.

The board has also received many applications that it deemed speculative. More than 110 applicants had requested over 30,000MW of electricity, but “only about a quarter or fewer had genuine investment plans,” it reportedly said.

Thailand attracted more than US$50 billion of investment-promotion applications in the first nine months of this year, out of which 70 per cent are AI-related, the board added.

Eligible projects approved before August 14 will be given one year to comply with the new guidelines.

stories.content:
Stockland and John Boyd Properties have dropped a data centre as a potential use from the amended masterplan for the former Kogarah Golf Club site in southern Sydney, opting to focus on a logistics precinct and mixed-use development.

The amended Concept Masterplan, which follows the original submitted earlier this year, no longer includes a data centre among the uses it covers. A Stockland spokesperson told W.Media the data centre had not progressed far enough to be included in the company’s data centre development pipeline.

“Stockland and John Boyd Properties are focused on the development of a world class logistics precinct which does not include a data centre as part of the amended Concept Masterplan,” the spokesperson said.

The company said the decision was business- and market-led. It said the site’s location near Sydney Airport, Port Botany and major transport infrastructure made it uniquely suited to logistics.

“The site is on the doorstep of Sydney Airport and in close proximity to Port Botany and major transport infrastructure, making it uniquely suited for a logistics hub and has potential for mixed uses, like retail and hospitality,” the spokesperson said.

Plans for the first building, known as Building 3A, will focus on logistics, with a planning submission expected as the next stage of the development progresses.

The wider redevelopment is also expected to deliver a one-kilometre public foreshore link along the Cooks River, the future delivery of the 14-hectare Pemulwuy Park, local road upgrades and improved active transport connections.

Stockland said it would continue engaging with stakeholders as planning for the logistics precinct progresses, including consultation on Building 3A.

### Stockland’s wider data centre pipeline

The Kogarah decision comes as Stockland continues to develop a broader data centre platform across its Australian property portfolio. In its 1Q27 Operational Update, released last month, Stockland identified seven potential data centre sites across NSW and Victoria, with about 450MW of power secured, subject to final design, documentation and customer negotiations.

The sites are MPark Stage 2, Kemps Creek, Wetherill Park and Macquarie Park in NSW, and Cherry Lane, Brooklyn and Melbourne Business Park in Victoria. Stockland identifies Cherry Lane and Brooklyn as having approximately 175MW of power secured each and MPark Stage 2 approximately 100MW. The other four sites are at application or planning stage.

Stockland holds a 100 per cent interest in MPark Stage 2, Cherry Lane, Brooklyn and Wetherill Park, a 50 per cent interest in Kemps Creek and Melbourne Business Park, and 51 per cent in Macquarie Park.

The company describes the sites as providing a multi-year development pipeline, with the majority located within established logistics precincts. It expects an initial funds from operations contribution in FY27 from land transfers and sales, with further contributions anticipated through land transfers, development gains, fee income and net operating income.

The company says it is continuing to progress additional power applications and planning across the portfolio.

COREWEAVE said on Tuesday (Nov 10) it would become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028, as the AI cloud company sought to reassure investors that strong demand and customer commitments will support its debt-fuelled expansion.

Shares of the Nvidia-backed company were up 5 per cent in extended trading after it also said it does not see any material risks to its data-centre buildout from a potential shift in regulatory landscape after the Democrats’ sweeping win in the US midterms.

CoreWeave shares have crashed more than 40 per cent in the past month after the firm emerged as the focal point of growing AI bubble fears, with investors worried about heavy borrowing for setting up data centres against the backdrop of rising interest rates and the pace of returns on the massive investments.

The steep selloff also triggered a broader crisis of confidence in the AI trade. Earlier in the day, AI juggernaut Anthropic kicked off a roadshow for its share sale at a lower target valuation than earlier estimates.

Easing some jitters, CoreWeave said it would not tap unsecured debt markets at current yields and that it had enough cash flow from existing customer commitments to repay current debt and any additional borrowing needed to fulfill those contracts.

CoreWeave had about US$46.9 billion in total debt as of the end of September. It expects to raise less than US$5 billion in additional capital through 2027.

CEO Mike Intrator said the company had US$9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits that will flow in over the next three months.

“Customer contracts come first, and investment follows. Because CoreWeave‘s investments are tied to committed demand, lenders have something concrete to lend against and customers typically help fund the buildout,” he said in a statement.

CoreWeave‘s revenue backlog stood at US$132.5 billion at September-end, rising from US$104 billion at the end of June. At the same time, its quarterly capital spending jumped to US$14.5 billion from US$9.4 billion in the prior quarter.

That spending is necessary to bring capacity online to meet the surging demand, CoreWeave said, as it is largely sold out of capacity through the next year, with about ten times as much demand as available capacity.

### No impact expected from changes in political landscape

Investors have been worried about tech companies’ data-centre expansion plans as they prepare for a tougher regulatory environment after the Democratic win in the midterm elections. Public backlash has already been growing in the US around data centres’ impact on local resources including water and power.

“There is going to be a lot more scrutiny on how you build, how you use resources... But I don’t think it’s going to require a material change in how we go about building our infrastructure. I don’t think it’s going to materially distort the costs of the buildout,” Intrator told Reuters in an interview.

“I do think that there is going to be a pacing issue, as people need to be more transparent and work through the process with the communities and that’s going to be prevalent across the industry. But that’s how we’ve done it historically and it has been a hallmark of how we’ve built our data centres.”

Intrator said that CoreWeave will not ramp up international expansion plans because of the election results.

“This is not a new strategy that you’ve got us building into as a reaction to the elections. This is something that we have been working at diligently for a year and a half already,” he said.

CoreWeave now expects 2026 revenue to be between US$13 billion and US$13.3 billion, from US$12.4 billion to US$13.2 billion earlier.

It also lifted the lower end of its annual spending target by US$2 billion, now projecting spending of US$37 billion to US$39 billion.

CoreWeave‘s third-quarter revenue surged nearly 170 per cent to US$3.66 billion, beating estimates of US$3.55 billion, while a per-share loss of 95 cents came in smaller than estimates for a US$1.16 loss, according to data from LSEG. REUTERS

REDWOOD CITY, Calif., Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Equinix, Inc. (Nasdaq: EQIX), the world's digital infrastructure company<sup>®</sup>, today announced that Equinix Europe 2 Financing Corporation LLC has issued €2.5 billion in aggregate principal amount of green senior notes across four tranches, which carry an effective all-in interest rate of 4.82% per year on a blended basis after the estimated impact of interest rate hedges. The notes are guaranteed by Equinix, Inc. This latest issuance is Equinix's largest green senior notes offering to date and underscores Equinix's continued commitment to integrate sustainability across its business and capital allocation strategies, helping fund projects that deliver measurable environmental impact across its global operations.

The offering closed on November 9, 2026. Including this latest issuance, Equinix has issued more than US$12 billion of green bonds globally, making it one of the top issuers in the investment-grade green bond market.

The proceeds from the offering are expected to be allocated to finance and/or refinance eligible green projects under Equinix's recently updated Green Finance Framework, which streamlines the eligible product categories and strengthens the company's approach to sustainable financing in alignment with internationally recognized market standards and best practices. The updated framework focuses investment across eligible project categories including green buildings, renewable and clean energy, energy efficiency, and sustainable water management and watershed resilience initiatives, advancing Equinix's decarbonization and resilience priorities as part of its long-standing commitment to sustainability.

"At Equinix, sustainability is deeply embedded in our business and capital allocation strategy," said Olivier Leonetti, Chief Financial Officer, Equinix. "The strong demand for this offering reflects investor confidence in our long-term growth strategy and supports investments through our Green Finance Framework that help deliver measurable environmental impact while creating lasting value for our customers, communities and stakeholders."

The issuance builds on Equinix's long track record in sustainable finance and follows the recent publication of the company's 2026 Green Bond Allocation and Impact Report, which provides transparency into the use and allocation of proceeds from prior green bond issuances. The report also confirms that, as of June 2026, 100% of proceeds from Equinix's outstanding green bond issuances had been allocated, with no remaining unallocated net proceeds.

stories.summary: Japanese multinational investment holding company SoftBank Group has reported its first quarterly net loss in almost two years after its subsidiary, Silver Bands 7 (SB7), was forced to swallow a US$ 3.7 billion write down attributed to its US data center projects while AI valuations dip globally. In its second quarter results SoftBank Group reported […]
stories.title_zh: Ohio数据中心电力设备减值致SoftBank亏损70亿美元
stories.content:
Japanese multinational investment holding company SoftBank Group has reported its first quarterly net loss in almost two years after its subsidiary, Silver Bands 7 (SB7), was forced to swallow a US$ 3.7 billion write down attributed to its US data center projects while AI valuations dip globally.

In its second quarter results SoftBank Group reported a net loss of US$ 7 billion after writing down payments to secure power-generation equipment for its 8 GW PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County, Ohio. The advance payment was non refundable and totaled US$ 2.85 billion, and a further US$ 880 million was paid for contract modifications and settlements.

In its results, SoftBank Group said its subsidiary SB7, which is also backed by SoftBank Vision Fund 2, had become entitled to receive rebates of up to US$ 2.1 billion over the next 10 years on future equipment purchases. The exact figure had not been determined as of September 30, 2026.

While net sales climbed 13.3 percent to US$ 26.4 billion, SoftBank Group swung to a half-year net loss of US$ 4.8 billion from a profit of US$ 20 billion a year earlier.

The company reported that it had invested US$ 20 billion in OpenAI in the first two quarters of its fiscal year. With an additional US$ 10 billion invested in October, SoftBank’s cumulative investment in OpenAI sits at US$ 64.6 billion for a stake of around 13 percent. SoftBank also acquired DigitalBridge Group, Inc. during the reporting period for US$ 3.1 billion.

“We can treat the loss from the review of the AI data center plans as temporary. The more worrying factor is the increase in financial cost,” Kazuki Sawamura, Shinkin Asset Management strategist, told Bloomberg. “If investment income and the value of its holdings don’t grow steadily from here, the interest burden could squeeze earnings and heighten concern about SoftBank’s financial health.”

Sharon Chen, a credit analyst at Bloomberg, said that after spending US$ 11 billion on data center investments in the first half of the year, there was a risk that uncertainty would increase.

stories.content:
Equinix has launched a new data center in Singapore, following nearly seven years of limited development due to the moratorium in the city-state.

Over the weekend, the Nasdaq-listed colo announced the opening of SG6, its sixth International Business Exchange (IBX) data center in Singapore.

Located in Jalan Tukang, the nine-story SG6 will provide approximately 1,550 cabinets in its first phase, and up to 20MW of IT capacity upon full build-out. Equinix has invested an initial $290 million in the project.

Equinix CEO Adaire Fox-Martin said: “Singapore sits at the intersection of global commerce, digital technology and sustainable development. Equinix has been investing in Singapore for nearly 25 years, and our new facility will further expand our presence as the neutral exchange where enterprises connect to the clouds, networks and partners they need to innovate and grow. Singapore is one of our most important markets globally, and our continued investment here is a testament to the central role it plays in the digital economy.”

Singapore has had a moratorium on new data center developments since 2019 (although already authorized facilities were allowed to be built after this point), but this is starting to be relaxed.

The facility was built under the Singapore Government's Data Centre – Call for Application (DC-CFA) process, which granted a limited amount of new capacity to a handful of operators. Equinix broke ground in November 2024, and the facility was originally due to launch in Q1 2027.

Yee May Leong, Singapore managing director for Equinix, added: "Singapore’s strength has always been its ability to look ahead - to embrace growth and innovation while being thoughtful about how we use our resources. I’m proud that Equinix can continue to play a part in Singapore’s growth, working alongside government and industry to enable the next generation of AI and innovation, while building a more resilient and sustainable future.”

SG6 incorporates on-site renewable energy generation through solar panels installed on the rooftop and the facade of the building. The site includes rainwater harvesting systems to reduce water use.

The new facility is designed to achieve a Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.20 and is targeting BCA-IMDA Green Mark Platinum certification. Aligned with Singapore's national standard for energy efficiency (SS 715:2025), customer IT server equipment deployed at SG6 must hold a recognized energy efficiency certification or demonstrate an equivalent level of efficiency.

Equinix, GDS (now DayOne), Microsoft, and a consortium of AirTrunk and TikTok-owner ByteDance were collectively allocated 80MW of new data center capacity in Singapore in 2023.

Equinix has operated in Singapore since 2002. Its previous Singapore facility, SG5, launched in 2021. The company was also one of four companies granted a new capacity in the second DC-CFA earlier this year.

Digital Realty, Equinix, Keppel Data Centers, and ST Telemedia Global Data Centers will each be allocated 50MW of new capacity under the second DC-CFA. Equinix has not detailed how that capacity will be used.

The new data center will also host a Co-Innovation Facility (CIF) in partnership with the National University of Singapore Energy Solutions Hub. Targeted to open in 2027, the facility will provide a platform to test and scale new cooling, digital twin, and energy and sustainability solutions.

stories.title: Vertiv partners with Infineon to scale power semiconductors for AI data centers
stories.summary: Vertiv has signed a three-year partnership with German semiconductor manufacturer Infineon Technologies to develop and scale the supply of silicon and silicon carbide power semiconductors.
stories.title_zh: Vertiv partners with Infineon to scale power semiconductors for AI data centers
stories.content:
Vertiv has signed a three-year partnership with German semiconductor manufacturer Infineon Technologies to develop and scale the supply of silicon and silicon carbide power semiconductors.

According to the companies, the strategic agreement will support supply continuity and reliable, on-time delivery as Vertiv scales production to meet growing demand for critical digital infrastructure. Vertiv said that the components will play a crucial role in the development of its 800VDC power systems.

The deal will expand an existing partnership between the two firms and is intended to support the integration of Infineon's semiconductors across Vertiv products worldwide.

Vertiv said it selected Infineon for its technical capabilities in insulated-gate bipolar transistor, silicon, and silicon carbide technologies, along with its global manufacturing capabilities and track record of quality.

“The rapid evolution of AI is reshaping the power requirements of the data center, and our customers need infrastructure partners who can anticipate what comes next,” said Frieda He, chief procurement officer at Vertiv. “This agreement strengthens our ability to deliver for customers today while supporting the next generation of power architectures required for AI and other critical applications. By aligning our technology roadmaps with Infineon – and securing access to critical power semiconductors – we are taking another proactive step that enables our customers to scale with confidence.”

“The agreement with Vertiv reflects our shared commitment to supporting the evolving requirements of critical power infrastructure,” said Andreas Weisl, EVP and chief sales officer, industrial and infrastructure at Infineon. “Through our comprehensive portfolio and manufacturing capabilities, we can provide Vertiv with the advanced power semiconductor technologies needed to support its continued innovation and growth.”

Infineon is one of Europe's largest semiconductor manufacturers. Spun out of Siemens in 1999, the company specializes in power electronics, automotive microcontrollers, sensors, and security chips. Recently, it increased its research and development in power infrastructure for the data center sector, partnering with Korean electrical equipment manufacturer LS Electric to develop direct current power infrastructure for the AI data center market earlier this year. It also recently inked a deal with Estonian power and storage systems supplier Skeleton Technologies to develop a suite of high-efficiency, resilient power solutions for modern data centers.

A major player in the data center supply chain, Vertiv has made several major acquisitions in 2026, including data center cooling firm ThermoKey, prefab enclosure maker Bmarko, and coldplate specialist Strategic Thermal Labs.

It has also announced several new designs aimed at AI data centers. In June, it launched Vertiv Rack Extreme, which it described as a “future-ready rack platform” that “supports deep and heavy IT equipment required for next-generation deployments.”

stories.title_zh: Microsoft 据称敦促 Trump 阻止预期的中国 data centre 技术禁令
stories.summary_zh: 据三位熟悉讨论情况的消息人士透露，Microsoft正在积极游说特朗普政府阻止一项预期的行政命令，该命令将禁止在美国数据中心使用中国制造的电力转换和配电设备。该公司认为，此类限制将扰乱供应链并延迟关键AI基础设施的建设，因为中国制造商在某些关键电气组件市场上占据主导地位。
stories.why_zh: Microsoft的干预暴露了西方AI基础设施战略中的一个关键脆弱性：对中国电气设备的依赖无法迅速替代。如果禁令实施，随着中国供应商将产出转向非美国市场，亚太地区的数据中心建设时间表可能会延长，全球供应趋紧。对于马来西亚、新加坡和澳大利亚的运营商而言，政策结果将影响他们是否面临来自美国买家寻求替代供应来源的竞争需求，可能推高区域设备成本。
stories.content:
Microsoft has been pressing the Trump administration to halt plans to bar Chinese imports of a key component used in AI data centres, three people familiar with the situation said.

*Reuters* reported in August that the Trump administration wants to ban US imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light within data centres.

The concern is that they could be used by Beijing to steal data, install malware or disrupt service at US data centres.

Microsoft has 35 data centres under construction in the US and another 134 planned, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company which tracks data centre development.

It is one of a group of companies and trade groups making the case to the Trump administration that such a ban could irreparably damage the US edge over China in the AI race by further slowing the data centre rollout, the sources said.

The cloud and software company was one of a handful of firms that met with officials from the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and the National Security Council in September to flag the supply chain challenges that any such ban would present, two of the sources said.

"It really threatens to arguably grind (the data center rollout) to a halt," said John Miller, general counsel of the Information Technology Industry Council (ITI), a tech lobbying group, which has publicly urged the administration not to move forward with a ban.

He said many cloud companies have already purchased the AI chips needed for the buildout. "Those chips, without optical transceivers literally could just sit there waiting around un-utilised until you actually have the transceivers to essentially connect them together," he added.

Some data centres need millions of optical transceivers to connect servers, routers and switches.

The US Federal Communications Commission, which oversees the US telecom industry, is working on the ban.

The efforts by Microsoft and other firms, which have not been previously reported, show how the agency's deliberations have set off alarms in an industry scrambling to meet surging demand for cloud and AI services despite a growing backlash by consumers over rising energy costs and water use.

Microsoft declined to comment. The White House, the FCC and the Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

### US competitors lack scale

China boasts two-thirds of the global market for optical transceivers, according to Counterpoint Research. Chinese firms like Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight, which was added to the Pentagon's list of Chinese military-backed companies, dominate global supply, counting top American hyperscalers among their customers.

US-based Coherent and Lumentum produce technology that competes with them but lack the scale to replace Chinese vendors, according to a report by the Foundation for American Innovation.

ITI sent a letter to the FCC on August 13 calling on the telecoms watchdog to "refrain from adding optical transceivers" to a trade blacklist, emphasising the "potential effects that supply disruptions could have on data centre deployment and US AI leadership."

Morgan Stanley said in an October client note that the Trump administration was considering barring Chinese optical transceivers capable of handling 3.2 terabits of data per second, whose production is not expected to ramp up until 2028, with widespread installation expected in 2029.

Such a threshold could avoid antagonizing US companies and Beijing while giving US optical companies time to expand production.

The FCC has not addressed the optical transceiver issue publicly, but two of the sources said the 3.2 terabit per second threshold is under consideration.

Lawmakers may not want to wait. In September, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers introduced legislation to bar the federal government from equipping sensitive government systems with Chinese-made optical transceivers.

stories.content:
MUNICH (Nov 10): Dutch chipmaker Nexperia is "totally oversubscribed" as suppliers divert manufacturing capacity towards fast-growing artificial intelligence (AI) data centres and away from the mature chips used in cars and industrial equipment, interim CEO Stefan Tilger told Reuters at the Electronica trade fair in Munich on Tuesday.

Tilger said some competitors had shifted capacity away from the commodity semiconductors supplied by Nexperia, creating bottlenecks in parts of the automotive supply chain.

"The automotive industry is suffering at the moment quite heavily," he said in an interview.

STMicroelectronics CEO Jean-Marc Chery warned on Monday that foundries and chip-packaging companies were increasingly shifting resources away from products used in automotive and industrial applications.

"We see many bottlenecks," Chery said at a CEO panel ahead of the conference on Monday.

The comments add to evidence that the AI investment boom is creating bottlenecks elsewhere in the semiconductor supply chain, as manufacturers prioritise higher-margin products linked to data centres and AI.

Some foundries and assembly and packaging firms that previously served a broad range of customers "are disengaging ... from mainstream technology", he said.

Tilger said demand from AI data centres and robotics was absorbing capacity, while investment in the mature technologies used for diodes, transistors and other basic components had lagged for years.

Nexperia specialises in high-volume, low-cost semiconductors used primarily in vehicles and industrial equipment. Unlike larger rivals such as STMicroelectronics, it has a narrower product range focused on mature-node components.

Chery said ST's own manufacturing footprint offered some protection from supply constraints.

"We control a part of our future with our capex and our manufacturing," he said.

South Korean telecommunications firm SK Telecom, AI chip startup Rebellions, and NVIDIA have announced a collaboration to advance South Korea’s AI infrastructure. This initiative aims to integrate data centers, processors, and an open infrastructure platform.Rebellions will use NVLink Fusion to connect its Rebel R200 neural processing units (NPUs) to NVIDIA’s infrastructure platform. SK Telecom plans to deploy these systems, leveraging its data center expertise, according to a press release from NVIDIA.Jung Jai-hun, SK Telecom Chief Executive Officer and President, stated this collaboration validates the potential of next-generation sovereign AI infrastructure. He added it combines global AI infrastructure technology with Korean AI semiconductors.Sunghyun Park, Rebellions co-founder and Chief Executive Officer, noted that Korean technology would lead in powering AI worldwide. Jensen Huang, NVIDIA founder and Chief Executive Officer, highlighted Korea's talent and ambition to be a world leader in AI.The firms plan to develop an approach to disaggregated inference. This will assign different stages of AI response generation to the best-suited processor architecture. The plan includes using NVIDIA GPUs for prefill and Rebellions NPUs for decode to improve inference throughput.
### Government Support and Investment

South Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) supports this collaboration to strengthen the country’s sovereign AI infrastructure. Bae Kyung-hoon, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT, said this enables Korean-developed NPUs to enter the computing infrastructure market alongside NVIDIA.The government will actively support this collaboration, he added, to deliver tangible results and advance cooperation with NVIDIA. Earlier this month, the South Korean government allocated KRW 21.3 trillion (US$ 15.83 billion) in its budget for 2027. This funding supports the development of physical AI, data centers, and semiconductors.A further KRW 4.7 trillion (US$ 3.5 billion) has been earmarked to develop a sovereign AI model. The government also plans to train 2,000 specialists to lead semiconductor design and the wider chip industry.

stories.title: Diraq deploys Australia's first quantum computer in Sydney
stories.summary: The eight-qubit machine is now live in Sydney, marking a move from laboratory research to commercial use and giving Australia its first quantum computer.
stories.title_zh: Diraq在悉尼部署澳大利亚首台quantum computer
stories.content:
Tue, 10th Nov 2026 (Yesterday)
Diraq has deployed Australia's first quantum computer in a commercial data centre at Equinix in Sydney. The system is now live with eight qubits.

The installation moves an Australian-built quantum machine out of a research setting and into a facility used for mainstream computing workloads across banking, healthcare, utilities, manufacturing and retail. Diraq plans to scale the deployed system to 256 qubits within the next year.

The machine occupies 16 square metres and draws less than 20 kW of power. Diraq says those requirements show quantum hardware can operate in existing data centre environments rather than requiring purpose-built sites.

Diraq builds silicon spin quantum systems using semiconductor manufacturing processes similar to those used for conventional computer chips. It says that approach would let customers expand computing capacity by upgrading the quantum processor while making only limited changes to the surrounding infrastructure.

### Data centre move

The Sydney deployment comes as quantum computing companies try to show their systems can be integrated into commercial technology estates rather than remaining confined to laboratories. Equinix says hosting the machine creates a path for quantum systems to connect with cloud, artificial intelligence and high-performance computing environments already used by corporate customers.

"We are now at a point where quantum computing can start to reach industries and the people they serve," said Andrew Dzurak, chief executive officer and founder of Diraq.

"That shift matters more than any single milestone, because it changes what's possible for every field quantum touches, from medicine to materials to logistics. Our silicon spin approach is what puts that within reach in five years, not decades. It gives us a manufacturing path already proven at industrial scale, a cost curve that improves as we add qubits, and a system designed to run inside today's existing computing infrastructure," Dzurak said.

Equinix described the deployment as a marker for the domestic quantum sector as companies try to bridge the gap between research and operational use.

"Diraq's deployment at Equinix represents an important milestone for Australia's quantum industry," said Jarrod Nink, managing director for Australia at Equinix.

"By hosting Australia's first quantum computer in a commercial data centre, we are helping bridge the gap between research and deployment, while creating the foundation for quantum systems to connect seamlessly with the cloud, AI and high-performance computing ecosystems that enterprises rely on today," Nink said.

### Medicine model

Alongside the deployment, Diraq released a report examining how quantum computing could affect industries including medicine, energy, materials, climate and transport. Part of the analysis focused on the economics of drug development.

Diraq says developing a new medicine can cost more than USD $2 billion and take up to 15 years, while fewer than one in 10 candidates reach patients. Based on modelling derived from an industry cost study published in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, it says a 10 percentage point rise in clinical trial success rates could result in about 50% more potentially lifesaving medicines reaching patients each year.

In a market the size of the United States, that would equate to as many as 25 additional medicines annually, according to the analysis. Diraq also says the same improvement could save USD $600 million per medicine by identifying failed candidates earlier, provided the quantum computer used to produce that result costs less than USD $65 million a year to run.

Diraq uses that threshold to argue that the economics of useful quantum systems will depend not only on scientific progress but also on whether operating costs remain below the value created for customers. It says many competing architectures become more expensive as they scale because they require more cooling, wiring and control equipment.

By contrast, Diraq says it is targeting utility-scale systems that would cost at most tens of millions of dollars. It also says a future utility-scale machine could draw around 300 kW, which it describes as less than a third of the power required by a single next-generation AI rack, and could shrink to as little as five square metres.

The deployment follows earlier support for the company's manufacturing plans in Australia from the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation. Diraq has also advanced to Stage C of DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, which carries potential funding of up to USD $300 million, and has signed a USD $38 million letter of intent with the US Department of Commerce under the CHIPS and Science Act.

"Advanced quantum technologies have already helped compound an estimated $19 to $27 trillion in value globally, and BCG estimates quantum computing could unlock a further $3.5 trillion at maturity," Dzurak said.

"It's clear that the companies that build real capability now will end up capturing that future value. This deployment is how Australia starts doing exactly that: proving research born here can be engineered and built to a global standard, with value that reaches people here and around the world," he said.

stories.content:
Speedmatrix reportedly received over 200 shipments of restricted tech between June 2024 and June 2025

\[JOHOR BAHRU\] Malaysia has not initiated an investigation into Speedmatrix, the Malaysian subsidiary of Singapore cloud provider Megaspeed, said Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Johari Abdul Ghani on Tuesday (Nov 10).

His comments followed a Megaspeed statement issued in December 2025, that institutions including the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) had conducted on-site inspections and reviews that found no evidence of illicit chip transfers or other illegal activities.

Johari told news portal Malaysiakini that the ministry had not been presented with evidence that Speedmatrix had contravened Malaysian law.

Credible evidence or a formal request from foreign authorities would be assessed under Malaysia’s laws and processes, he said, adding that the country would not allow itself to be used as a channel to circumvent export controls.

In a statement dated Dec 23, 2025, responding to a Bloomberg report, Megaspeed said it had undergone “multiple on-site inspections and reviews” over the preceding six months by institutions including the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, Miti and Nvidia. It denied wrongdoing.

*The Business Times* has asked Miti whether it conducted the checks cited by Megaspeed, which facilities they covered, what they found and whether these efforts were part of a formal investigation.

As at press time, BT has not received a response.

Megaspeed is under scrutiny over whether it helped to channel restricted Nvidia chips to China. Bloomberg has reported that the US Justice Department is investigating Megaspeed.

Nvidia’s board has also opened an independent investigation into whether its CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The move follows reports about his relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US intelligence agencies reportedly believe is a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia’s board said it had no reason to believe that company secrets or national security had been compromised.

Speedmatrix received more than 200 shipments of Nvidia technology restricted from export to China between June 2024 and June 2025, *The New York Times* reported last year, citing trade records.

Separately, Megaspeed’s Malaysian expansion plans include a proposed data centre in Bandar Cemerlang Industrial Park in Kota Tinggi, Johor. It is undertaking this through MSFusion, which Bursa Malaysia-listed developer Crescendo Corp referred to in stock exchange filings as another Megaspeed subsidiary.

In an Aug 27 filing, Crescendo Corp disclosed that its subsidiary’s solicitors had issued a default notice to MSFusion over RM225.9 million in outstanding principal payments under an agreement to buy 52.54 acres of land.

MSFusion was given 14 days from Aug 27 to remedy the default, failing which the seller would be entitled to terminate the agreement. On Sep 9, Crescendo announced that the balance purchase price and late-payment interest up to Aug 26 had been fully paid to its solicitors.

That announcement did not identify the source of funding.

Bloomberg separately reported in April that Bridge Data Centres had told lenders in February that 68.4 megawatts of capacity previously earmarked for Megaspeed at one of its Malaysian facilities had been reassigned to cloud provider Zenlayer.

BT has sought comment from Megaspeed on its Malaysian operations and MSFusion’s project, and from Crescendo on the land transaction.
